quick.summary: How to design pipelines that you can safely restart when they break.
quick.takeaway: Make your pipeline safely repeatable by replacing the time window instead of adding.

beats.line: My pipeline failed halfway. I ran it again, and now everything is duplicated. Why?
Think of a smart thermostat. You tell it to heat the room.
If I press the button twice, it does not get twice as hot.
Right. It just ensures the target state is reached.
Pipelines should act the exact same way.
We design them to be strictly idempotent.
Can I just say safely repeatable?
Perfect. Running the job twice must give the same result as once.
But how do I stop it from adding the same rows again?
You have to clean the slate before you draw.
Like wiping the whiteboard before writing a new list?
Exactly. Before your pipeline inserts today's data, it should delete today's data.
If the job failed yesterday, the cleanup catches any partial mess.
That feels dangerous. What if I delete the wrong thing?
You only target the specific time window you are replacing.
Never drop the whole table. Just drop the affected hours.
So I clear out the bad hours, then write them fresh.
You will never fear a retry again.

quiz.question: How do you make a daily pipeline safely repeatable?
options: Never run the pipeline more than once a week.
Add the new rows on top of the old rows every time.
Delete the specific time window before inserting new rows.
Delete the entire table and start over.
quiz.explanation: Cleaning out the specific hours you are replacing prevents duplicates without harming the rest of the table.

quiz.question: A safely repeatable pipeline means it does the exact same thing whether you run it once or ten times.
quiz.explanation: Just like a thermostat, it ensures the final state is correct no matter how many times you press the button.
